title: Conditional sentences

objectives.can: Classify a condition by the mood and tense of its verbs and say what it supposes.

explanation.summary: A Latin conditional sentence shows by the mood and tense of its verbs what the speaker supposes. The indicative leaves the matter open. An imperfect subjunctive supposes something that is not true now, a pluperfect subjunctive something that did not happen. Read the verbs first, then the English 'would'.

sections.heading: The parts of a condition
body: A conditional sentence has two clauses. The 'if' clause is the protasis, and it begins with *si* ('if') or *nisi* ('unless', 'if not'). The main clause, which says what follows, is the apodosis. In Matthew 12:27 the protasis is *si ego in Beelzebub ejicio dæmones* and the apodosis is the question *filii vestri in quo ejiciunt?*

The two words for 'not' differ in scope. *nisi* denies the whole condition and often means 'unless'. *si non* denies one word, usually the verb or a word near it. In Matthew 24:22 *nisi breviati fuissent dies illi* is 'unless those days had been cut short'. In Matthew 26:24 *si natus non fuisset homo ille* is 'if that man had not been born'. Both forms occur in the Vulgate.

sections.heading: The indicative: an open condition
body: When both clauses are in the indicative, the condition is open. The speaker neither says it is true nor that it is false. Matthew 12:27 has *si ... ejicio* in the present, and John 8:46 has *si veritatem dico vobis, quare non creditis mihi?* 'if I speak the truth, why do you not believe me?' Jesus assumes the condition for the argument.
The main clause need not be an indicative. It can be an imperative or a command. In John 8:39 the apodosis is *opera Abrahæ facite*: 'if you are children of Abraham, do the works of Abraham'.

For the future, Latin uses a future perfect for the 'if' clause and a future for the main clause. Matthew 6:14 reads *Si enim dimiseritis hominibus peccata eorum: dimittet et vobis Pater vester*: 'if you forgive people their sins, your Father will forgive you'. The ending *-eritis* belongs both to the future perfect indicative and to the perfect subjunctive, so the library's automatic analysis cannot always tell them apart. Here the future main verb *dimittet* shows that the 'if' verb is a future perfect indicative. The same holds for *nisi abundaverit* in Matthew 5:20.

sections.heading: The imperfect and pluperfect subjunctive: not true
body: A condition with the subjunctive in both clauses can suppose something that is not so. If both verbs are imperfect subjunctive, the supposition is about the present: John 14:28 has *Si diligeretis me, gauderetis utique*: 'if you loved me, you would rejoice'. The speaker suggests that this is not the case. John 8:42 has the same pattern: *Si Deus pater vester esset, diligeretis utique et me*.

If both verbs are pluperfect subjunctive, the supposition is about the past. Martha says *Domine, si fuisses hic, frater meus non fuisset mortuus* (John 11:21): 'Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died'. She means that he was not there and her brother did die. In 1 Corinthians 2:8 the pattern is *si enim cognovissent, numquam Dominum gloriæ crucifixissent*: 'if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory'.

The tenses may be mixed when the time of the two clauses differs. John 15:22 has two pluperfects in the 'if' clause and an imperfect in the main clause: *Si non venissem, et locutus fuissem eis, peccatum non haberent*. The past supposition (if I had not come and spoken) has a result that holds now (they would not have sin). Matthew 23:30 combines a pluperfect ('if we had been') with an imperfect ('we would not be').

sections.heading: The present subjunctive in an 'if' clause
body: Classical Latin uses the present subjunctive in both clauses for a remote or less likely future: 'if he should come, he would see'. The Vulgate has the present subjunctive in some 'if' clauses, but it is looser and does not always follow this pattern. In Matthew 16:26 the clause is *si mundum universum lucretur, animæ vero suæ detrimentum patiatur*, 'if he should gain the whole world and suffer the loss of his soul'. The main clause is a question in the present indicative, so the sentence supposes a case without asking us to read it as unlikely.

In 1 John 1:9 *Si confiteamur peccata nostra: fidelis est* the 'if' verb is a present subjunctive and the main verb an indicative. Classical Latin would use the indicative here. So in the Vulgate a present subjunctive after *si* tells you only that the case is a supposition, and you must read the main clause and the context for more.

The apodosis can also be a subjunctive of the kind met in the first lesson of this stage, such as a command. In Matthew 27:42 *si rex Israël est, descendat nunc de cruce*: 'if he is king of Israel, let him come down from the cross now'.

misunderstandings: Reading an imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive in an 'if' clause as simply past. The tense pair supposes something unreal: imperfect for the present, pluperfect for the past.
Treating the indicative as proof that the condition is true. An open condition leaves the question open, as the argument in John 8:46 shows.
Translating by the English 'if I were' alone. Look at the Latin verbs, as English uses 'were' and 'would' for several different cases.
Assuming that every *-erit* or *-eritis* form after *si* is a subjunctive. In a future condition it is usually the future perfect indicative.
Taking *nisi* and *si non* as the same. *nisi* often means 'unless', while *si non* denies one word.

deeper.heading: Other ways of sorting conditions
body: Some grammars classify conditions by the speaker's view of the facts (simple, contrary to fact), others by time and vividness (future more vivid, future less vivid, present general, past general). The forms they describe are the same. This lesson uses the names that follow the forms. When a grammar gives a different name, find the verbs first and the label will follow.

examples.analysis: *ejicio* in the 'if' clause and *ejiciunt* in the question that follows are present indicatives: an open condition. Jesus does not say he casts out demons by Beelzebub. He assumes it for the sake of the argument and turns it against his questioners.

examples.analysis: *dimittet* is a future indicative in the main clause. With a future main verb, the verb of the 'if' clause, *dimiseritis*, is a future perfect: if you forgive (shall have forgiven), your Father will forgive you. The analysis in this library lists *dimiseritis* as a perfect subjunctive and does not teach from it, as the form is ambiguous.
